content: Trachoma is a significant cause of preventable blindness, particularly in underprivileged populations in many developing countries. Approximately 146 million people are estimated to have active trachoma, and nearly six million individuals are blind due to complications arising from repeated infections. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the impact of promoting face washing as a preventive measure for active trachoma in communities where the disease is endemic. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted, including CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, PubMed, LILACS, and others, covering studies published up to January 2015. No restrictions were applied regarding language or publication date. Additional trials were identified by reviewing reference lists, using citation tracking, and consulting experts in the field. The final search of electronic databases was performed on January 26, 2015. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs that compared face washing with no treatment, or face washing combined with antibiotics versus antibiotics alone. Participants were residents of trachoma-endemic communities. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed the quality of the trials. When necessary, trial authors were contacted for further information. Due to methodological differences between the included studies, a meta-analysis was not conducted. Two cluster-RCTs met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 2,447 participants. These trials were conducted in trachoma-endemic regions: Northern Australia and Tanzania. One trial had a follow-up period of three months, while the other followed participants for 12 months. Both trials achieved approximately 90% follow-up at the final visit. However, the overall quality of the evidence was uncertain due to incomplete reporting of study design methods and variability in the outcomes reported between the trials. In one trial, face washing combined with topical tetracycline was compared to topical tetracycline alone in three pairs of villages. After 12 months, the combination of face washing and topical tetracycline was found to reduce severe active trachoma compared to tetracycline alone (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 0.62, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.40 to 0.97). However, no significant difference was observed between the intervention and control villages in reducing other forms of active trachoma (adjusted OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.59). Additionally, children in the intervention villages had a higher prevalence of clean faces compared to those in the control villages, both among children with severe trachoma (adjusted OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.59) and among those with any trachoma (adjusted OR 0.58, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.72) at the 12-month follow-up. The second trial evaluated the effects of eye washing compared to no treatment, topical tetracycline alone, or a combination of eye washing and tetracycline drops in children with follicular trachoma. At three months, the trial found no evidence that eye washing alone or in combination with tetracycline eye drops reduced follicular trachoma in children (risk ratio [RR] 1.03, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.11; one trial, 1,143 participants). In conclusion, evidence from one trial suggests that face washing combined with topical tetracycline may be effective in reducing severe active trachoma and increasing the prevalence of clean faces after one year. However, the current evidence is inconclusive regarding the effectiveness of face washing alone or in combination with topical tetracycline in reducing active or severe trachoma. Further high-quality research is needed to clarify these findings.
